replying_to: Replying to Vulnerable Agent Identification in Large-Scale Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
display_title: Official Review of Submission11855 by Reviewer gNJg

summary.value:
This paper proposes a new problem formulation of adversarial attacks in large scale multi-agent reinforcement learning. The problem formulation focuses on adversarial attacks of mean field control. The attacker can select a subset of agents to be adversarial and design an adversarial policy for them with bounded similarity against the intact policy. Adversarial agents execute that adversarial policy, and the rest agents are victims which execute the intact policy.

This paper further proposes a bi-level hierarchical algorithm to solve the problem: (1) on the upper level, the algorithm incrementally selects adversarial agents following the objective of minimizing the worst performance that can be achieved with the selected agents as adversarial; (2) on the lower level, given the subset of adversarial agents selected by the upper level, the algorithm finds adversarial policies for them that can lead to the worst performance. The lower level problem is solved by mean-field Bellman operator derived from Fenchel-Rockafellar duality. The effectiveness of the algorithm is empirically justified by out-performing baselines on 17 of 18 tasks of finding the strongest adversarial attack under the problem formulation.

strengths.value:
The problem formulation of adversarial attack in large scale multi-agent reinforcement learning proposed by the paper is useful for diagnosing the robustness of a policy: The set of worst case adversarial agents can indicate which agent is vulnerable, and the worst performance can reveal the robustness of the policy.

The paper proposes an effective algorithm to tackle the problem, justified by their empirical study. Moreover, the mean-field Bellman operator derived from Fenchel-Rockafellar duality can efficiently estimate the worst performance given the set of adversarial agents, in terms of both accuracy and running time.

weaknesses.value:
1. The impact of this paper is limited, as:

(a) it only studies under the setting of mean field control, which assumes agents are heterogeneous and can be approximated by mean field approximation. This assumption is no longer true under the setting of adversarial attack, where the behavior of adversarial agents are different from victim agents;

(b) in the problem formulation (Assumption 3.2), the difference between adversarial and intact policies of each adversarial agent is bounded by the same factor $\epsilon$. This formulation excludes adversarial attack where different adversarial agents are perturbed by different $\epsilon^i$. The latter can potentially lead to stronger adversarial attacks that are hard to detect in terms of overall behavior of all agents;

(c) the paper is limited to tasks with discrete action space.

2. Estimation of upper level reward faces sampling error caused by sampling trajectories. The paper lacks the analysis of how error in estimating upper level reward affects the performance of the adversarial attack. The paper can be better if make both theoretical and empirical discussion on this.

3. In empirical evaluation, environments are quite simple (scale of state and action is not big). It is unclear how the method performs in more complicated environments.

4. A few places are not well written, which makes the paper difficult to understand:

Line 197: How is the trajectory collected?

Line 266: Why is the first inequality true? By definition, $(\hat{\mathcal{B}}^{\hat{\pi}}V^i)(s^i,\mu)=\min_{\pi_\alpha}(\mathcal{B}^{\hat{\pi}}V^i)(s^i,\mu)\le(\mathcal{B}^{\hat{\pi}}V^i)(s^i,\mu)$. Also there may be a typo at the end of line 264.

Figure 1: What do scattered points and curves mean?

Table 1: What is the rule to bold text? It should be consistent, e.g. only bold the best method.

questions.value:
1. Can the method be extended to find adversarial attacks for more general multi-agent reinforcement learning set up: (a) no assumption of heterogeneous agents; (b) potentially different $\epsilon^i$ for different agents; and (c) multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks with continuous action space?

2. Is there a bound for the error in estimating upper level reward? How many trajectories need to be collected to ensure the error is within an acceptable range? How does the performance (overall reward of following adversarial-attacked policy) change with respect to magnitude of error?

3. How does the method perform in more complicated environments, e.g. SMAC[1]?

4. Please address confusing parts in writing that are mentioned in **Weaknesses**.

5. In Table 1, VAI-Greedy is better than VAI-RL on some tasks. Do the authors have any insight on why this happens?

[1] Samvelyan, Mikayel, et al. "The starcraft multi-agent challenge." arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.04043 (2019).

comment.value:
We thank Reviewer gNJg for appreciating the problem formulation, algorithm design and theoretical derivation of our paper. A detailed response is provided below.

> Q1: The paper only studies under the setting of mean field control, which assumes agents are heterogeneous and can be approximated by mean field approximation. This assumption is no longer true under the setting of adversarial attack, where the behavior of adversarial agents are different from victim agents;

Please allow us to clarify that our paper investigates the question of controlling large-scale cooperative MARL algorithms, where mean-field control offers state-of-the-art solution to this problem, which assumes agent behaviors can be approximated by mean-field approximation.

As for the different behaviors of victims and adversaries, [1] proof the mean-field assumption is valid for agents with different objectives in Section 3.1 of their paper, so mean-field approximation holds for cases with victim and adversaries. Our work thus evaluates provides a principled foundation of examing the vulnerable agents in mean-field control.

[1] Mean Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning. ICML 2018.

> Q2: In the problem formulation (Assumption 3.2), the difference between adversarial and intact policies of each adversarial agent is bounded by the same factor $\epsilon$. This formulation excludes adversarial attack where different adversarial agents are perturbed by different $\epsilon^i$. The latter can potentially lead to stronger adversarial attacks that are hard to detect in terms of overall behavior of all agents.

Please allow us to clarify that our theory applies to attackers with different $\epsilon^i$. To show this, our Propositions 4.1, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.4 all considers $\epsilon^i$ explicitly. Our previous assumption 3.2 makes a mistake for assuming each agents having the same perturbation budget, which is not required. We have updated assumption 3.2 in Line 201 to alleviate this.

However, please allow us to clarify that we assume attackers having the same $\epsilon^i$ in experiments since this allows us to study the problem with controlled variable. Our theory do not have such limitations.

> Q3: The paper is limited to tasks with discrete action space.

Please allow us to clarify our Vicsek environment operates in continuous action space, where each flock selects an continuous angle to navigate. We have clarified this in Line 398-399.

> Q4: Estimation of upper level reward faces sampling error caused by sampling trajectories. The paper lacks the analysis of how error in estimating upper level reward affects the performance of the adversarial attack. The paper can be better if make both theoretical and empirical discussion on this.

Regarding the error induced by approximations, we add a remark in Line 315-323 to reflect this. The dual formulation in Proposition 4.2 relies on the Fenchel–Rockafellar transform, which is exact whenever the underlying uncertainty set is convex, proper, and lower semicontinuous. As shown in Proposition 4.1, our uncertainty set is $\ell_p$-bounded, which naturally satisfies these conditions. Therefore, the Fenchel–Rockafellar transform yields the exact optimal value of the inner minimization over adversarial perturbations, rather than a relaxation or bound. In practice, when $Q^i$ is approximated by a neural network, any discrepancy between $Q^i$ and the optimal robust value arises solely from standard function-approximation and Bellman-residual errors, and propagates in the same way as in conventional robust RL—not from the Fenchel–Rockafellar transform itself. Notably, this exactness property depends only on the convexity structure of the uncertainty set and does not require the value function or the policy to be convex.

> Q5: In empirical evaluation, environments are quite simple (scale of state and action is not big). It is unclear how the method performs in more complicated environments. How does the method perform in more complicated environments, e.g. SMAC?

Please allow us to clarify that our environments are not that simple. First, take Battle with 64 agents as an example, the state space is 289 dimension and action space is 25 dimension, which is comparable to SMAC in both state and action scales.

Second, Battle is similar to the setting of SMAC, where two group of agents competes with each other. The action space is also similar, containing moving and attacking enemies. With large number of agents, adding complex environment dynamics like SMAC makes the game computationally hard to solve, which motivates MAgent to design a SMAC-like task with simpler environment dynamics.

Finally, SMAC tasks contains ~10 agents and are designed for MARL algorithms like MAPPO which models each agents separately and can achieve precise control. This do not fit mean-field MARL with ~100 agents and the goal is to verify the capability of controlling large-number of agents. As such, large-scale MARL and common cooperative MARL are two different fields, and SMAC for cooperative MARL may not fit large-scale MARL well.

> Q6: How is the trajectory collected? How many trajectories need to be collected to ensure the error is within an acceptable range?

The trajectories are collected by performing 100 rollouts using the fixed, pre-trained cooperative policy $\pi_\beta$. We have add this to the manuscript. In our pilot study, we have tried collecting 1000 rollouts for comparison, but the performance do not improve further, so we deem 100 rollouts are sufficient for estimating the value function under attack. We have clarified this in Line 1124-1125.

> Q7: Why is the first inequality true? Also there may be a typo at the end of line 264.

The inequality comes from Lemma 3.2 in the seminal paper of Iyengar [1]. Here, $V^i(s^i, \mu)$ is the value function under worst-case perturbation. For the robust value function to be feasible, we must have $V^i(s^i, \mu) = (\hat{\mathcal B}^{\hat{\pi}} V^i)(s^i, \mu) = \min_{\pi_\alpha}(\mathcal B^{\hat{\pi}} V^i)(s^i, \mu) \leq (\mathcal B^{\hat{\pi}} V^i)(s^i, \mu)$, which means the robust value function must have smaller value than Bellman functions with perturbations that are not in the worst-case. However, we do find some notations to be incorrect and have corrected Eqn. 9 and 10 correspodingly. As for the end of line 264, we admit that *robust feasible inequality* is not commonly used, and we change it to *robust Bellman inequality* to adhere to the norms in [1] explicitly. We have updated related details in Line 270-287.

We have double-checked proofs for Proposition 4.2, and it is correct.

[1] Robust Dynamic Programming. Mathematics of Operations Research 2005.

> Q8: Figure 1: What do scattered points and curves mean?
 
The scattered points represent the results for verifying the accuracy of our regularized mean-field Bellman operator. While the operator is designed to predict the reward under attack, we explicitly plot the predicted value of our regularized mean-field Bellman operator (y axis) and the actual value of running that attack (x axis). The curves represents a linear correlation, with shaded area the 95% confidence interval. The high $R^2$ values (0.97, 0.91) show a strong Pearson correlation. We have updated the caption of Figure 1.

> Q9: Table 1: What is the rule to bold text? It should be consistent, e.g. only bold the best method.

In Table 1, our proposed method includes VAI-Greedy and VAI-RL. We bold the text when our method outperforms all baselines. We will make it clear in our revision.

> Q10: In Table 1, VAI-Greedy is better than VAI-RL on some tasks. Why?

Please refer to Line 438-442 for this discussion. VAI-RL outperforms VAI-Greedy when more attackers are available. Since our regularized mean-field Bellman operator in Proposition 4.2 is already an accurate approximation of the original problem. As such, with less number of agents, the immediate reward estimation is accurate and agent-wise interaction is weak, so we can use Greedy algorithm to find a good approximation directly. In contrast, when there are large number of attackers, RL can better model the long-term returns and inter-agent relationship, resulting in stronger attack capability.

summary.value: This paper explores the detection of individual agents that could potentially have a significant impact on the performance of all other agents if taken over by an adversary. The authors formalize this problem as a bi-level optimization problem: the upper level selects the most vulnerable agents and the lower level learns the worst-case policies for those agents. They demonstrate that selecting the most vulnerable agents is NP-hard and that learning adversarial policies is a mean-field multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) task. The authors additionally propose a practical algorithm and demonstrate the effectiveness of attacks conducted using their approach.

strengths.value:
1. The paper explores identifying vulnerable adversaries by assuming weaker adversaries and larger-scale systems than previous work. This results in a relevant problem with reasonable threat modeling.
2. The assumptions are clearly stated and well-defined. The assumptions used in the experiments are reasonable.
3. The method is derived from a regularized mean-field Bellman operator and is shown to learn the optimal selection of vulnerable agents and adversarial policies.
4. The empirical evaluation of the method is extensive and shows strong results in three environments.

weaknesses.value:
1. Including more complex environments, such as the ones chosen here, would be beneficial. Currently, it is unclear how the method scales to more complex systems. However, I don't think this is a significant issue given the compelling nature of the current experiments.
2. It would have been interesting to see qualitative results showing how the policy of an adversarial agent differs from that of a benign one. Specifically, can the selected agents only degrade performance because they were originally achieving high rewards, or can they also influence other agents in the system to perform poorly?
3. I find the paper's writing to be slightly confusing. The abstract and introduction read more like a paper on detecting vulnerable agents as a defense mechanism, while the methods and experiments are written more like an attack against MARL systems. The authors should update their writing or presentation of the results to address this discrepancy.
4. Related to the previous point, investigating simple defense methods would contribute to the paper. For example, one could investigate adversarial training methods, in which agents are trained alongside adversarial agents in the same environment.

questions.value:
1. What does the behavior of an adversarial agent look like on a qualitative level? Can they influence other agents, or are they simply the most effective agents in the system?
2. How do you envision the practical application of this method? Is it intended to be an attack method against large-scale systems or a defense mechanism against adversarial policies?

We thank Reviewer vLJ8 for appreciating the novelty of our problem definition, reasonable assumptions, method design and empirical evaluation of our paper. A detailed response is provided below.

## Response

> Q1: Including more complex environments, such as the ones chosen here, would be beneficial. Currently, it is unclear how the method scales to more complex systems. However, I don't think this is a significant issue given the compelling nature of the current experiments.

Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that evaluating the method on more complex environments would further strengthen the work. At this stage, implementing additional mean-field MARL environments is challenging because many of them do not have open-source implementations, and reproducing them from scratch requires substantial engineering effort. Moreover, several complex environments are computationally demanding due to the large-scale multi-agent dynamics inherent to mean-field MARL, making extensive experimentation difficult within the conference timeline.

We appreciate the reviewer’s insight and fully agree that broader experimental coverage would provide additional value. We are currently preparing an extended journal version of the paper, where we plan to include more complex and computationally intensive environments to examine our method in a more comprehensive way.

> Q2: It would have been interesting to see qualitative results showing how the policy of an adversarial agent differs from that of a benign one. Specifically, can the selected agents only degrade performance because they were originally achieving high rewards, or can they also influence other agents in the system to perform poorly?

Our adversaries are able to influence other agents negatively. This is discussed in Section 5.2, "Second, the failure of one agent can negatively affect others". In Battle, disruption of selecting the adversary with the highest value affects other agents in the same row unable to coordinate forward and attack the enemies, while in Taxi, the agents to the left are blocked by the adversary and unable to reach the center area with highest reward. We will expand the subsection "Second, the failure of one agent can negatively affect others" to include more discussions on this.

> Q3: I find the paper's writing to be slightly confusing. The abstract and introduction read more like a paper on detecting vulnerable agents as a defense mechanism, while the methods and experiments are written more like an attack against MARL systems. The authors should update their writing or presentation of the results to address this discrepancy.

We have updated the abstract and introduction in our paper to reflect our VAI is an adversarial attack that can be used by defenders to proactively identify and defend against the subset of agents whose compromise would most significantly degrade overall performance. We hope this revision would better clarify our motivation. The updates are made in Line 12-15, and Line 50-52.

> Q4: Related to the previous point, investigating simple defense methods would contribute to the paper. For example, one could investigate adversarial training methods, in which agents are trained alongside adversarial agents in the same environment.

Thanks for raising this important problem for discussion. Examing the defense for our VAI algorithm raise critical theoretical challenge. As the victim policy evolves, the group of vulnerable agents for the current system change as well. As such, the optimal solution of this problem is an equilibrium for selected vulnerable agents, such that the attacker and defender cannot gain more reward by selecting other group of vulnerable agents, as well as an equilibrium for victim policy and attack policies, such that the attacker and defender cannot gain more reward by altering their agent policy.

However, designing such defense mechanisms can involve significant more theoretical derivations and is considered as our future work. To address your concern, we have add defense to each agent using the action regularizer proposed by ERNIE [1]. The action uncertainty yields a ERNIE regularizer of the form $R(s, a, \mu, \nu) = \max_{||\nu - \nu_{\alpha}|| \leq  \epsilon} \sum_{a \in \mathcal A} ||Q(s, a, \mu, \nu) - Q(s, a, \mu, \nu_\alpha)||$. 

Using $\epsilon = 8/64$, we observe that ERNIE is effective at improving the robustness of mean-field MARL algorithms, while our VAI methods consistently outperforms other attacks. ERNIE is not fully effective as a defense method since it assumes fixed number of adversaries in its neighbourhood, which is not effective with our VAI that selects the group of most vulnerable agents, which can be more than 8/64, where the defense is insufficient, or less than 8/64, where the defense is overly pessimistic. 

However, note that these results are prelinminary and do not reflect the optimal defense, and we choose not to include these in our revision. Due to the theoretical complexity in designing optimal defenses for VAI, we leave a formal, rigorious investigation of defense methods as future work.

> Q5: How do you envision the practical application of this method? Is it intended to be an attack method against large-scale systems or a defense mechanism against adversarial policies?

Thanks for the suggestion to illustrate our point using a potential application as motivation. We have included the following example in our Introduction session:

In a thousand-robot swarm, individual robots may encounter action uncertainty from software or hardware errors, environmental hazards, or even be controlled by adversaries. These individual failures can ultimately lead to the failure of the entire team; In a power grid with hundreds of nodes, failure of certain nodes can trigger cascading failures, leading to a large-scale blackout. As agent policies are interconnected in mean-field MARL, it is crucial for defenders to proactively evaluate the impact of the failure of a small group of agents on the entire system, with worst-case failure generated by adversarial attack. The updates are made in Line 12-15, and Line 44-47.

summary.value: Given a set of agents, this paper presents an approach to identify the most vulnerable subset, including the subset identification and the training of an adversarial policy for that subset. The problem is modeled and studied theoretically, and two algorithms are proposed (a RL approach, and a greedy approach). Experiments are then performed in 3 different domains.

strengths.value:
- The problem is interesting and relevant.

- The theoretical study and the model seems ok.

- The results are significantly better than baselines.

- Additional analysis are conducted to help explain the results.

- The writing is clear, overall.

weaknesses.value:
By coincidence, I already reviewed an earlier version of this paper, and my main concerns of the previous version were (i) only the case \epsilon = 1 was studied, when the attacker has full control over the subset of agents; (ii) the computational cost was not studied; (iii) there were typos and grammar issues in the text, although the writing overall was ok; (iv) the source code was not available at that time.

I see that in this version the authors released the source code anonymously, and added appendix D.1 and appendix D.2, with the study of the computational cost, and the study of different values of \epsilon (i.e., different levels of control by the attacker).

However, these new additions seem to have been added somewhat quickly, and a few issues still remain:

- In appendix D.1, which environment was used? And what is the variance, confidence interval, etc? Also, only 2 cases are studied, so it is hard to say how it scales as the agent number grows.

- In appendix D.2, the variance is also not shown. Additionally, authors run experiments only in one environment (Battle), while the experiments in the main paper uses 3 environments. It is unclear why we would study different values of \epsilon only in the Battle environment.

- Additionally, the text in the appendix has several writing issues, e.g.:

-- "agents) since it do not requires additional training.", "Our VAI-RL is fast since it do not need"-> "it does not"

-- "First, VAI-RL works constantly better for VAI-Greedy" -> you meant "VAI-RL works constantly better than VAI-Greedy"?

-- "the result also shows our VAI-RL and VAI-Greedy works better in various perturbation budgets ϵ" -> You meant better than baselines?

-- "the effect of our VAI is consistent with this constained budget." -> You meant "constrained"?

Hence, in general, although the paper does have new additions, they seem rushed, and are not in the same level of quality as the previous experiments in the main paper.

questions.value:
- Which environment was used in appendix D.1?

- What is the variance of the results in appendix D.1 and D.2? Are the results statistically significant?

- Why only study different values of \epsilon in the Battle environment? Would the results still be positive in different environments?

## Response

We sincerely thank reviewer for the detailed feedback and the support of accepting our paper in the previous round. We have added all suggestions by reviewers in previous round, and have carefully incorporated all suggestions of reviewers in this round into our final version.

> Q1: In appendix D.1, which environment was used? And what is the variance, confidence interval, etc? Also, only 2 cases are studied, so it is hard to say how it scales as the agent number grows.

We use **Battle environment** for Appendix D.1 since it was most commonly used in literature. Following your suggestions, we have added the variance in our revision and included all tasks in Battle environment for comparison, with 5 random seeds. To our surprise, the computation cost of all baselines is generally manageable ($\leq$ 2 hours), except in scenarios with a very large number of adversaries (144 agents with 72 adversaries), where mean-field MARL training itself becomes the primary computational bottleneck. Please refer to Appendix D.1 for the update. We have also updated the main paper in Line 448-455 to summarize our main findings.

> Q2: In appendix D.2, the variance is also not shown. Additionally, authors run experiments only in one environment (Battle), while the experiments in the main paper uses 3 environments. It is unclear why we would study different values of \epsilon only in the Battle environment.

In Appendix D.2, we use Battle environment as a representitive task for our study. Following your suggestions, we have added addditional experiments in Taxi, with 50 agents and 25 adversaries, and 100 agents with 50 adversaries, with all results shown in 5 random seeds. We find VAI-RL and VAI-Greedy consistently outperform all baselines, with statistically significant improvements ($p<0.05$) under the Friedman test. Moreover, VAI-RL surpasses VAI-Greedy when $\epsilon$ is small and the proportion of adversaries is relatively large, demonstrating the advantage of reinforcement learning in capturing synergistic interactions among coordinated adversaries. Please refer to Appendix D.2 for the update. We have also updated the main paper in Line 456-461 to summarize our main findings.

> Q3: The text in the appendix has several writing issues.

Thanks for the detailed review for enhancing our paper, which makes our paper significantly more rigorous. We have carefully revised the grammar in our revision.

summary.value: This paper studies an optimal attack problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). The authors consider the setting where a subset of the agents can be attacked, whose policy will be modified by the attacker with certain budget constraint. The authors show that this optimization problem is NP-hard. The authors propose a method that efficiently solves the lower-level problem for finding the worse-adversary policy. For the upper-level problem, the authors formulate the corresponding combinatorial optimization problem into an MDP problem, which can then be solved using standard RL algorithms.

strengths.value:
1.	This paper provides a complete study of the problem, including its complexity analysis and algorithm design and analysis.
2.	Comprehensive numerical results are provided to support the performance of the proposed algorithm.

weaknesses.value:
1. The motivation of the attack model introduced in Section 3.1 needs some further explanation. In particular, why the perturbed attack model is considered, and why the adversary faces a budget constraint $\epsilon^i$ (i.e., is there any physical meaning of this constraint on the adversary)? Does the adversary need to now the agent’s original policy $\pi_{\beta}^i$. In general, a worst-case adversary could potentially alter the agent’s original policy in an arbitrary manner.

2. Proposition 3.3 and its proof need to be checked again. In particular, when you want to prove a problem is NP-hard, the reduction is from a known NP-hard problem to the problem that you want to prove. The direction seems to be reversed in the paper.

3. While the authors prove that the optimization problem in Eq.(2) is NP-hard, the authors the prove in Proposition 4.5 that the algorithm they propose solve the problem optimally. Either the algorithm proposed is not a polynomial algorithm or the solution must lose optimality. An explicit analysis of the computational complexity (e.g., run time) of the proposed algorithm needs to be provided. In addition, in Section 4.2, the authors propose a greedy-type algorithm, i.e., at each step $k$, the algorithm selects the most vulnerable agent, adds it to the selected set of vulnerable agents, and proceeds to the next step. In general, such kind of greedy algorithm for NP-hard optimization problem would return only an approximate solution. Based on the above, it would be good to check again the result in Proposition 4.5 and its proof.

4. Typos: line 325, is it correct to refer to Eqn. 4.2? line 286, to prove that.

comment.value:
We thank Reviewer Mzaz for appreciating the comprehensive study of VAI problem and comprehensive experiments for our paper. A detailed response is provided below.

## Response

> Q1: The motivation of the attack model introduced in Section 3.1 needs some further explanation. In particular, why the perturbed attack model is considered, and why the adversary faces a budget constraint $\epsilon^i$ (i.e., is there any physical meaning of this constraint on the adversary)? Does the adversary need to now the agent’s original policy $\pi^i_\beta$. In general, a worst-case adversary could potentially alter the agent’s original policy in an arbitrary manner.

The threat model of our attacker assumes a perturbed policy is $\hat{\pi}^i = \epsilon^i \pi^i_\alpha + (1-\epsilon^i)\pi^i_\beta$, which is motivated by [1]. $\epsilon^i$ can be understand as how much the perturbed policy deviates from the original policy, such as the policy face a change in its weight, friction, etc, and is connected to $\ell_p$ bound. In this formulation, the adversary do not require assess to victim's policy, and $\epsilon^i$ is only a bound to reflect how much the policy deviates from victim policy. If worst-case adversary could potentially alter the agent’s original policy in an arbitrary manner, it corresponds to the case of $\epsilon^i = 1$, and $\hat{\pi}^i = \pi^i_\alpha$. Our main experiments in Table. 1 considers this case explicitly. We have added related clarifications in Line 157-160.

[1] Action robust reinforcement learning and applications in continuous control. ICML 2019.

> Q2: Proposition 3.3 and its proof need to be checked again. In particular, when you want to prove a problem is NP-hard, the reduction is from a known NP-hard problem to the problem that you want to prove. The direction seems to be reversed in the paper.

Thanks for pointing out. We have revised our proof to correct our reduction direction from maximum coverage problem to our upper-level problem. The high-level idea is the same. The revised proof is updated in Appendix. A.1.

> Q3: While the authors prove that the optimization problem in Eq.(2) is NP-hard, the authors the prove in Proposition 4.5 that the algorithm they propose solve the problem optimally. Either the algorithm proposed is not a polynomial algorithm or the solution must lose optimality. In addition, in Section 4.2, the authors propose a greedy-type algorithm, i.e., at each step, the algorithm selects the most vulnerable agent, adds it to the selected set of vulnerable agents, and proceeds to the next step. In general, such kind of greedy algorithm for NP-hard optimization problem would return only an approximate solution. Based on the above, it would be good to check again the result in Proposition 4.5 and its proof.

Please allow us to clarify that in Proposition 4.5, we prove that *The optimal solution of upper-level problem and lower-level problem combined is an optimal solution of the original HAD-MFC*, so in principle the optimal solution of the hierarchical decomposition yields the same optimal solution to the original problem. In the proof sketch, we have also claimed that we only proof *the existence of optimal solutions in upper-level and lower-level problem*. To avoid misunderstanding, we have changed the caption of Proposition 4.5 to **Decomposition is Optimality-Preserving**, and updated the proof sketch to explicitly state this.

As for the error induced by approximations, we add a remark in Line 315-323 to show our Proposition 4.2 is exact, so the error arises solely from standard function-approximation and Bellman-residual errors, not from the estimatiton process in Proposition 4.2. Additionally, our theory depends only on the convexity structure of the uncertainty set and does not require the value function or the policy to be convex.



> Q4: An explicit analysis of the computational complexity (e.g., run time) of the proposed algorithm needs to be provided.

Please allow us to clarify that we have included this discussion in Appendix D.1 and Section 5.1, Computational Efficiency. We find while our VAI requires training an additional function in Proposition 4.2, the overall computation cost is on par with our baselines.


> Q5: Typos: line 325, is it correct to refer to Eqn. 4.2? line 286, to prove that.

In fact, our regularized mean-field Bellman operator is indeed defined in Eqn 4.2 and Proposition 4.3 write the same regularized mean-field Bellman operator with a change of variable only. We have revised our Proposition 4.2 in line 284 to include an explicit definition of our regularized mean-field Bellman operator to avoid misunderstanding.

summary.value:
The paper studies the problem of Vulnerable Agent Identification in the context of large-scale MARL, using the mean-field formalism. The reviewers recognized the paper as interesting and novel, however the overall sentiment of the reviews is negative.

The reviewers raised multiple concerns and asked clarification questions, which authors addressed in the responses during the rebuttal as well as through revisions of the manuscript. One of the important concerns that remained unaddressed was raised by reviewer gNJg, who pointed out a discrepancy between assumptions underlying mean-field MARL formulation may not hold under the adversarial attack that selects as subset of agents and makes them behave differently than the rest of the population. The authors' response does not really address the concern, as they did not present a clear argument that mean-field assumptions are valid in their adversarial setting.

While the paper has been improved through the revisions (and it's already a resubmission according to reviewer vdaB), I do not believe it fully ready for publication when there is uncertainty / lack of clarity around the core assumptions behind the analysis.

reviewer_concerns.value:
- The authors nicely summarized all reviewer concerns in https://openreview.net/forum?id=UtxvBiujPB&noteId=R0Foe6EXpL.
- The major unaddressed concern is related to the validity of the assumptions of the mean-field RL in the proposed adversarial setting. The brief justification offered by the authors is not sufficient as it does not resolve ambiguity around potential inconsistencies in their analysis.
